content: The document outlines a comprehensive framework and assessment tool designed to facilitate the engagement of all relevant healthcare providers in the management of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) at the country level. This tool, developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), aims to support national tuberculosis programs (NTPs) in implementing public-private mix (PPM) strategies for DR-TB care. The tool is structured to collect data, assess current capacities, and identify steps to expand PPM activities for DR-TB management. Key Highlights: 1. Purpose and Scope: The tool is intended to assist countries in achieving universal access to quality diagnosis and treatment for all tuberculosis (TB) cases, including DR-TB. 2. Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (DR-TB): DR-TB includes multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), and other forms of drug resistance. MDR-TB, characterized by resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin, remains a significant global health challenge. In 2013, an estimated 480,000 people developed MDR-TB, with 210,000 deaths attributed to TB worldwide. Despite improvements in detection, treatment capacity remains insufficient, with only 97,000 eligible patients receiving MDR-TB treatment in 2013. The global treatment success rate for MDR-TB is low, at 48%. 3. Public-Private Mix (PPM): PPM refers to partnerships between public and private healthcare sectors to enhance TB care. This includes collaborations between government ministries, private practitioners, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and other stakeholders. The tool emphasizes the importance of involving non-NTP providers in DR-TB management while maintaining the leadership role of NTPs. 4. Assessment Tool Structure: The tool is divided into five parts: Part A: Overview of the TB epidemiological situation and NTP performance. Part B: Current PPM activities for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB). Part C: Programmatic management of DR-TB (PMDT). Part D: PPM for DR-TB. Part E: Summary and conclusions. It includes a questionnaire to gather qualitative and quantitative data, assess existing capacities, and identify gaps in DR-TB management. 5. Objectives: The tool aims to: Collect information on current PPM activities and PMDT, focusing on non-NTP healthcare providers. Identify steps to initiate or expand PPM for DR-TB. Suggest new approaches for public-private collaboration in DR-TB management. 6. Challenges and Recommendations: The document highlights the slow progress in expanding DR-TB care and the need for strategic data collection to guide program expansion. It stresses the importance of standardized monitoring, collaboration with private providers, and addressing gaps in treatment capacity. 7. Implementation and Monitoring: The tool provides guidance on data collection, interpretation, and the development of actionable strategies. It also emphasizes the need for training, capacity building, and ensuring a reliable drug supply for DR-TB treatment. 8. Collaboration Models: The tool encourages the identification of potential partners among private providers and the evaluation of existing public-private collaboration models. It also includes a checklist to assess the readiness of private providers to manage DR-TB. 9. Policy and Practice: It also highlights the importance of pharmacovigilance and the management of adverse drug reactions (ADRs). 10. Capacity Building: The tool underscores the need for human resource development (HRD) plans, training materials, and supervision mechanisms to enhance the capacity of both NTP and non-NTP staff in DR-TB management. 11. Patient-Centered Care: The document emphasizes the importance of addressing the physical and emotional suffering of MDR-TB patients, ensuring access to free diagnosis and treatment, and evaluating patient satisfaction. 12. Strategic Expansion: The tool advocates for a strategic and efficient expansion of DR-TB management, guided by carefully collected data and collaboration with all healthcare providers. In summary, this WHO-developed tool serves as a critical resource for countries aiming to strengthen their DR-TB management programs through effective public-private collaboration, comprehensive data collection, and strategic planning. It provides a structured approach to address the challenges of DR-TB care and move towards universal access to quality treatment.
